THE DEATH OF THE PRESIDENT.
Winle celebrating the fall of Richmond and
the capture of Lee and his army, we did not
believe greater news possible; but greater
news,-or, at any rate, news that more
profoundly moved the whole nation, - came last
Friday tiight. We believed that the slave
power and its malignant horde of barbarians
had exhibited the whole extent of their
capacity for crime; but, though already a loathing
to civilization and an astonishment to devils,
they have added a still more horrible
illustration of their depravity. The only event in
History that can even be thought of as a
parallel to the assassination of President Lincoln

is the assassination of William Prince of
Orange, who was shot July 10, 1584, by a
creature of the most cruel and horrible
barbarism of that day.
N > purer or truer man than Abraham
Lincoln has ever lived. In all the land there was
not a more earnest, devoted, and
incorruptible patriot; and it has been well said that
a tenderer and nobler spirit never put down a
rebellion. Ho had earned the love and rev
erence of all true friends of this republic; and
they were given to him in the largest
measure. No president of the United States was
ever called to a work so great, trying, and
responsible, as that which he has done so
nobly during the last four years. He lived to
see the power of the rebellion broken, and to
hail the dawn of peace. His work is now
Gnished; his fame is secure; and not only the

people of this nation, but good and true men
everywhere will keep bis memory green
through all coming time. HU character and
his administration of the presidential office
will be among the most attractive themes of
the historian, and brighten with a pure and
steady light some of the noblest and most
exciting pages in our history.
But we do not propose to undertake a
eulogy of the late president. All the people
know very well what he was and what he did;
and the universal grief shows how fully lie
was understood,and appreciated. The
traittorous creatures of the desperate and dying
slave power, insane with malignity, have
assassinated the m in from whose clemency they
had most to hope; thus, seemingly, taking
pains to show all Christendom how little they
deserve mercy, and how much the welfare of
this nation requires their extermination.

This, very naturally, leads us to enquire,
what may the nation and the rebel
conspirators expect from Andrew Johnson, President
Lincoln's successor? Some answer to this
question is the more necessary, at this time,
because there are good- and earnest people
who are thinking more ot one recent fault of
his than of \\ifi great ability, hU strong
character, and his heroic loyalty that has been
tested in the furnace blast and shown to be
without alloy.
At the very beginningof the organized
conspiracy that produced this rebellion, Mr.

Johnson stood up against it, "steadfast as a
wall of brass." At that time he was in the
national senate; and no one who saw his
spirit, or listened to his words in the senate,
during the closing scenes of the Buchanan
administration, is likely to question his loyalty,
or forget the noble courage and wonderful
force with which he acted against the
conspirators, who had on their side not only the
administration and the slave power, but also
all the leading influences of the political partv
to which he belonged. A. H. Stevens, of
Georgia, could speak against secession
treason, and then weakly yield to it, and become
one of its foremost agents. Not so Andrew
Johnson of Tennessee. He deGed and fought
it at the beginning; he has defied and fought
it ever since, frequently at the peril of hTs life.

We have taken some pains to be well
informed in regard to the character and spirit of
Mr. Johnson, and we have entire confidence
in him. We believe that his administration
of the government, particularly in its
relations with the rebellion, will most agreeably
surprise and delight those who are led to
entertain doubts and anxieties, by their sense of
that "one fault," which, let us say, is
contrary to his habits and not likely to be
repeated. In fact, we do earnestly believe that
there are but few, very few men in the nation
as well fitted as he for the work now
committed to his hands. His great force of mind
and character, bis large acquaintance with
public affairs, and bis thorough knowledge
and appreciation of the rebel leaders and their
unpardonable crimes, qualify him to do this

work as the welfare of the nation requires.

j President Johnson's Policy.
Washington, April 16. - At a meeting
here of gentlemen of lowa, in relation to
president Lincoln's death, governor Stone
reported the substance of conversation with
president Johnson, as follows : -
"President Johnson said that while he
would deal leniently and kindly with the mass
of the people ol the south, and the rank and
tile ot their armies, he would be careful not
to pursue any p liey that would prevent the
government from visiting condign punishment
on the guilty authors of the rebellion. He
regarded it as due to the loyal people of the
country, and to the memory of the thousands
of brave men who have fallen in defence of
the Union, during this struggle, and to the
claims of justice and freedom throughout the
world, that treason should still be regarded as
tbe highest crime under the constitution and

flag, and that treason should be rendered
infamous for all time to come.
While he entertained these views, he should
endeavor to gain the confidence of the
deceived and betrayed masses of the southern
people, r**gaiding them as the proper material
for reconstructing the insurgent slates. He
would neither recognize nor hold official
communication with those who had occupied
official stations, or acknowledged the
sovereignty ot the rebel government. For 4 years
he had fought the rebel government with
all the energy of his character; he well Jtnew
the horrible outrages to which loyal citizens in
the south had been subjected, and it was his
determination to act in such a manner as
w<>uld best protect individual rights and
vindicate the character of the government. He
expressed deep sympathy with the betrayed
and deluded mrsses of the south, earnestly
desiring their return to their allegiance to the

government, and the restoration of their
former peace and prosperity. £
Gov. Stone expressed himself highly
gratified with these views of the presidet, and
predicted that the expectations of the true friends
of the country would be fully realized in the
wisdom, firmness and patriotism, which will
characterize President Johnson's
administration; and that the sentiments uttered by him
will find an earnest response in the people of
the great west.
Miscellaneous Report* and Fact*.
Washington, April 15. - About eleven
o'clock last night two men crossed the
A.iacostia bridge, one of whom gave his name as
Booth, and the other as Smith. The latter is
believed to be John Surratt. Last night a
riderless horse was found, which has been
identified by the proprietor of one of the stables
previously mentioned as having been hired
from his establishment. Accounts are
conflicting as to whether Booth crossed the

bridge on horseback or on foot, but as it is
believed he rode across, it is presumed that
he had exchanged his horse.
From information in possession of the
authorities it is evident that the scope of the
plot was intended to be much more
comprehensive. The vice president and other
prominent members of the administration were
particularly inquired for by suspected parties,
and their precise localities accurately
obtained ; but, providentially, in their cases the
scheme miscarried.
A boat was at once sent down the Potomac
to notify the gunboats on the river of the
awful crime, in order that all possible means
should be taken for the at rest of the
perpetrators. The most ample*precautions have
been taken, and it is not believed the
culprits will long succeed in evading the
overtaking arm ot justice.

There is no confirmation of the report that
the murderer of the president has been
arrested. Among the circumstances tending to
fix a participation in the crime on Booth, were
letters found in his trunk, one ot which,
apparently from a lady, su; plicated him to
desist from the perilous undertaking, in which
he was inauspicious, the mine not yet being
ready to be sprung.

I General Burnside on Andrew Johnson.
General Burnside was accosted Saturday
morning in William street, by some friends
who chanced to remember that during the
general's western command he was brought
into intimate contact with Andrew Johnson,
then military governor of Tennessee, and
must, therefore, know much about the
character of the citizen who, by the death of Mr.
Lincoln, suddenly becomes the head of the
nation. Gen. Burnside was therefore asked:
"Can we trust Andrew Johnson? Is he a
drunkard, as has been said?" The general
replied: "I know Mr. Johnson well. He
was military governor of East Tennessee
when I commanded in the West. For some
lime he was in Louisville and Cincinnati,
where I met him at all hours of the day and
night, and in most important consultations,
and I can say that I never saw him taste
liquor of any kind, and never saw him when I

thought lie had tasted liquor. He was no
drunkard then. In my opinion, he is a firm,
loyal and talented statesman" - JV. Y.

Sergeant J. M. Dye, of Battery C,
Pennsylvania artillery, discloses some
new facts in the following letter to his
father in New York :
Washington, April 15, 1865.
Dear Father With sorrow I pen
these lines. The death of President
Lincoln has deeply affected me. And
why shouldn't it, when I might have
saved his precious life 1 I was
standing in front of the theatre when the
two assassins were conversing. I heard
part of their conversation. It was not
sufficiently plain for an outsider to
understand the true meaning of it; yet it
apprised Sergeant Cooper and myself
that they were anxious that the
President should come out to his carriage,
which was standing just behind ns. The
second act would soon end, and they
expected he would come out then. I stood

a while between them aud the carriage,
with my revolver ready, for I began to
suspect them. The act ended, but the
President did not, appear ; so Booth
went into a restaurant arid took arinnk,
and then came out and went into the
aiiey where his horse was then standing,
though J did not know that any horse
was there, lie came back and
whispered to the other rascal, then stepped into
the, theatre. There were at this time
two police officers standing by them. I
was invited by my friend C. to have
some oysters, and we went into a saloon
around the corner, and bad just got
seated when arman came running in and
said the President was shot. This so
startled us that we could hardly realize
it, but we stepped out and were soon
convinced.

The 4th of March was fixed originally
for the assassination, and Booth was on
the ground, but either through fear of
not being able to effect his escape, or
because of the failure of his accomplice
to meet him at the time, the attempt
was not made. He is now known to
have waited for the President on that
day, on the embankment near the north
wing of the capitol, close to which Mr.

Lincolu would pass. He was dressed
shabbily in a slonchy suit, his
pantaloons crammed into his boots, and an
old felt hat pulled down over his face.
One of his acquaintances passing,
hailed him, but Booth pretended not to
hear and refused to speak until closely
approached. When the President passed
him, he hurried away, evidently
disappointed, and during the day vns gruff
and moody to all who had addressed
him. Being a coward, he hesitated to
strike the blow then, since he knew that
he would have instantly been torn to
pieces by the thousands present to
witness Mr. Lincoln's Inauguration. The
more investigation pries into the
murder the more dastardly it appears. It
was as cold and deliberative
assassination as the world ever knew.

Prospects for a General Hospital at
Fort Ensiling.
The prospects for a general hospital at
Fort Snelling are very encouraging. Dr.
E. Swift, of Milwaukee, Medical Director
of the Department of the Northwest, has
telegraphed to Governor Miller to know
whether buildings were now obtainable at
Fort Snelling for the purposes of a
general hospital. The Governor has replied
affirmatively, and strongly urged Dr.
Swift to establish a general hospital at
that post.
If this result can be accomplished (a
result which the different executives of the
State have been seeking for two or three
years,) it will be a boon of great value to
our State and her soldiers and soldiers'
relatives. Sick soldiers can then be
transferred to a hospital where they will
not only have the invaluable advantage of
our healthy climate to aid in their rapid

recovery, but their wives or relatives can
(with very small expense) visit them and
nurse them - attentions that often save
lives that would otherwise be lost.
It is sincerely to be hoped that a
general hospital will be established here. It
will be good news to thousands of our
people.
Poor Crazy Sherman
The radicals do not like Gen. Shebman.
They have never had any affection for him,
aud to do him justice, he has never had
any particular regard for them. Early in
the war, when commanding in Kentucky,
with a full knowledge of the resources of
the South, he expressed the opinion that
it would take two hundred thousand men
to drive the rebels out of Kentucky and
Tennessee. The radicals pronounced him
crazy, and sent him into retirement, where
he remained for nearly a year. Gen.

Grant, who knew his worth, subsequently
succeeded in getting him a command in
his own army, and when promoted to
Lieutenant General, he gave him command of
the combined armies of the Mississippi, of
the Ohio, and of the Cumberland. The
splendor of his achievements compelled the
radicals to join in the honors bestowed
npon him, while in their secret hearts they
hated him, because they could not use him
in furtherance of their negro-worshipping
schemes, and for what the rebels termed
his "fanatical love for the old Union,''and
for his oft repeated expressions ot regard
for the people of the South who were not
in arms against the government.

We have watched his course with great
interest, and have felt sure that the time
would come when the malignants would
be on his track again. They are after him
now like blood hounds, for no other reason
than this, that in making an agreement
for the immediate restoration of peace
%nd Union, he scorned the idea of
unnecessary humilition to the South, or of
exacting any other conditions than such as
he had been fighting for, ever since the
war commenced, viz., the restoration of
the Constitution and laws over the whole
country, and'the subjection of every
citizen to their requirements.

But we have no desire to discuss the
terms of the agreement. Gen. Sherman
transcended his authority - his action was
disapproved, very properly, perhaps, by
the government - and this is the end of
the matter. But we do enter our protest
against any impeachment of his motives
or of imputations upon his loyalty, or
upon the insinuations ot crazy fanatics
that he is not of sound mind. The
verdict of posterity may establish the fact
that his comprehension of the situation
and its requirements was more enlightened
and far-reaching than that of any other
man of the ago.

Men who address popular assemblies assume
a responsibility for the right use of the
influence and opportunities. If they arouse the
nobler sentiment of mankind, they do well.

If they make impressive events the occasion
for appealing to the dire passions of humanity,
they use them to brutalize and debase. The
heart must be lightly touched by the national
affliction, which can find relief in thoughts

We expect the American people to do their

at another moment the extreme of bloody
vengeance, which cries havoc. The wav to
either of these extremes is by reaction from

insurrection.

l am here, my friends and fellow citizens,

Rev. Henry Ward Beecher delivered an
elaborate and elegant address. Beginning
with a general review of the 'desolations
wrought by four years of war, he defined
the course for the exaltation of the nation
over the defeat of the rebellion.
The long night, he said, is ended, " and
for this returning day we have come from
afar to rejoice and give thanks. No more
war, no more accursed secession, no more
slavery that spawned them both. [Great
applause.] Let no man misread the
meaning of this unfolding flag. It says
government hath returned hither; it proclaims in
the name of vindicated government, peace
and protection to loyalty, humiliation and
pain to traitors. This is the flag of
sovereignty. The nation, not the States, is
sovereign, restored to authority. The
flag commands, not supplicates. There
Si ay be pardon, but no concession. [Great

pplause.] There may be amnesty and
oblivion, but no houied compromises.
[Applause.] The nation to-day has peace
for the peaceful, and war for the
turbulent." [Applause.] He added : "All that
we ask is unswerving loyalty and universal
liberty [applause], and that in tlie name
of this high sovereignty of the United
States of America we demand, and that,
with the blessings of Almighty God, we
will have. [Great applause.]
We raise our father's banner, that it may
bring back better blessings than those of
old; that it may dust out ( tbe devil of
discord ; that it may restore lawfal
government and a prosperity purer and more
endnring than that which it protected
before ; that it may win parted friends from
their alienationthat it may inspire hopt
and inaugurate universal liberty; that i
may eay to the sword, return to thy

sheath, and to the plough and sickle, go
forth; that it may heal all jealousis, unite
all policies, inspire a new national life,
compact onr strength, purify our
principles, ennoble onr national ambition, and

make this people great and strong; not
for aggression and quarrelsomeness, but
for the peaoe of the world, giving to us
the glorious prerogative of leading all
nations to juster laws, to more humane
policies, to sincere friendship, to rational
instituted civil liberty, and to universal
Christian brotherhood. Reverently,
piously, in hopeful patriotism, we spread this
banner on the sky, as of old the bow wa*
planted on the cloud, and with a solemn
fervor beseech God to look upon it and
make it the memorial of an everlasting
covenant, and decree that never again on
this fair land shall a deluge of blood
prevail. [Applause.]
Mr. Beecher prooeeded to show that the
war was begun by arrogant conspirators,
and charged its whole guilt upon " the
ambitious, educated, plotting political
leaders of the South," adding: "A day
will come when God will reveal judgment

and arraign at his bar these mighty
miscreants, and then every orphan that their
bloody game has made, and every widow
that sits sorrowing, and every maimed and
wounded sufferer, and every bereaved
heart in all the wide regions of this land,
will rise np and come before the Lord to
lay upon these chief culprits of modern
history their awful witness, and from a
thousand battlefields shall rise up. armies of
airy witnesses, who, with the memory of
their awful sufferings, shall confront these
miscreants with shrieks of fierce
accusation, and every pale and starved prisoner
shall raise his skinny band in judgment.

Blood shall call ont for vengeance, and
tears shall plead for justice, and grief shall
silently beckon, tbe heart smitten shall
wail for justice, good men and angels will
cry out how long, O Lord, how long wilt
thou not avenge? And then these
guiltiest and most remorseless traitors, these
high and onltured men with might and
wisdom used for the destruction of their
country, these most accursed and detested of all
criminals that have drenched a continent
in needless blood, and moved the
foundations of their times with hideous crimes
and cruelty, caught up in black clouds fall
of voices of vengeance and lurid with
punishment, shall be whirled aloft
and plnnged downward forever and
forever, in an endless retribution, while
God shall say, thus shall it be with all who
betray their country, and all in heaven
and upon earth will say, amen. [Voices

- ame*h, amen!] But for the people
misled - for the multitude drafted and. driven
into this civil war - let not a trace of
animosity remain. [Applause ] The moment
their willing hands drop the musket and
they return to their allegiance, then stretch
out your own honest right hand to greet
them. Recall to them the old days of
kindness. Onr hearts wait for their
redemption. All resources of a renovated
nation shall be applied to rebuild their

The prospeets for a general hospital at
Fort Snelling are very encouraging. Dr.
E. Swift, of Milwaukee, Medical Director
of the Department of the Northwest, has
telegraphed to Governor Miller to know
whether buildings were now obtainable at
Fort Snelling for the purposes of a
general hospital. The Governor has replied
affirmatively, and strongly urged Dr.
Swift to establish a general hospital at
that post.
If this result can be accomplished (a
result which the different executives of the
State have been seeking for two or three
years,) it will be a boon of great value to
our State and her soldiers and soldiers'
relatives. Sick soldiers can then be
transferred to a hospital where they will
not only have the invaluable advantage of
our healthy climate to aid in their rapid

recovery, but their wives or relatives can
(with very small expense) visit them and
nurse them - attentions that often save
lives that would otherwise be lost.
It is sincerely to be hoped that a
general hospital will be established here. It
will be good news to thousands of our
people.
Poor Crazy Sherman
The radicals do not like Gen. Sherman.
They have never had any affection for him,
and to do him justice, he has never had
any particular regard for them. Early in
the war, when commanding in Kentucky,
with a full knowledge of the resources of
the South, he expressed the opinion that
it would take two hundred thousand men
to drive the rebels out of Kentucky and
Tennessee. The radicals pronounced him
crazy, and sent him into retirement, where
he remained for nearly a year. Gen.

Grant, who knew his worth, subsequently
succeeded, in getting him a command in
his own army, and when promoted to
Lieu"tenant General, he gave him command of
the combined armies of the Mississippi, of
the Ohio, and of the Cumberland. The
splendor of his achievements compelled the
radicals to join in the honors bestowed
upon him, while in their secret hearts they
hated him, because they coaid not use him
in fartheranoe of their negro-worshipping
schemes, and for what the rebels termed
his "fanatical love for the old Union,''and
for his oft repeated expressions ot regard
for the people of the South who were not
in arms against the government.

We have watched his course with great
interest, and have felt sore that the time
would come when the malign ants would
be on his track again. They are after him
now like blood hounds, for no other reason
than this, that in making an agreement
for the immediate restoration of peace
%nd Union, he soorned the idea of
unnecessary bmnilition to the South, or of
exacting lany other conditions than such as
he bad been fightiQg for, ever since the
war commenced, viz., the restoration of
the Oonstitation and laws over the whole
oonntry, and the subjection of every
citizen to their requirements.

Bat we have no desire to discuss the
terms of the agreement. Gen. Sherman
transcended his authority - his action was
disapproved, very properly, perhaps, by
the government - and this is the end of
the matter. But we do enter onr protest
against any impeachment of his motives
or of imputations upon his loyalty, or
upon the insinuations ot crazy fanatics
that he is not of sonnd mind. The
verdict of posterity may establish the fact
that his comprehension of the situation
and its requirements was more enlightened
and far-reaching than that of any other
man of the ago.

The papers are teeming with aoooonts of

In referring to the violent demonstrations
in New York, the Times says: "We fear
there have been cases in which the
avenging of the deceased President has been a
mere pretext - the real impelling motive of
assault being the safe gratification of
private malioe or vengeance." To such an
extent have these exhibitions of private
vengeance been carried, that nearly all the
Administration journals of character and
influence have deemed it a duty to
condemn the outrages and their instigators.
The Oinoinnati Gazette, a radical paper, in
an article headed " Oratorical Looseness,"
says:
Men who address popular assemblies assume
a responsibility for the right use of the
influence and opportunities. If they arouse the
nobler sentiment of mankind, they do well.

If they make impressive events the occasion
for appealing to the dire passions of humanity,
they use them to brutalize and debase. The
heart must be lightly touched by the national
affliction, which can find relief in thoughts
of terrible satisfaction on the murderer; and
they must be lacking in moral sense who can
use such an occasion to appeal to popular
vengeance ; who strive with each other In stirring
up the passions of the audience, and who,
exaggerating thir own feelings with the applause
of the excited assembly, drive passion to the
top of their bent.

We expect the American people to So their
dnty in the settlement of this war, and to
provide indemnity for the past and security for

capacity for this would be the reaction between
the extreme of moral and political weakness,
at one moment, which would throw away the
lesson of the past with all its terrible cost, and
would surrender all security for the future, and
at another moment the extreme of bloody
vengeance, which cries havoc. The way to
either of these extremes is by reaction from
the other. It will require more substantial
stuff than either to settle the affairs of this
insurrection.

make this people great and strong; not

An immense meeting was held in the
Academy of Music in Brooklyn last
Monday night, to express the sorrow of the
people for the death ol President
LinOOUT. Several clergymen addressed the
meeting and lond calls were made for
Gborok Francis Train, who was pres.
ent. He came forward and. with his
usual fondness for opposing the
sentiments of his andienee, made some
reference to Christ's "Sermon on the Mount"
and quoted "Blessed are the merciful for
they shall obtain mercy." The
sentiment was hissed, and Train took his
ilit.

The general tone of the speeches seems
to have been identical with some that
we have heard of in this vicinity, and
the Brooklyn Eagle comments upon the
doctrine inculcated, in a manner so just
and forcible that, considering the
similarity of sentiment here, we cannot
refrain from copying a portion of the
artists
"The Bev. Dr. Vinton was the chief
speaker at the Academy last evening.
He is a man of estimable character, and
he belongs to a profession, the purpose
of whose members it is, or ought to be,
1 to calm the passions of men. Dr.
VinJ TON'S speech, so to speak, gave tone to
the meeting. He selected for the
edification ol the meeting a story from the
Bible, not generally turned to by those
who seek in the sacred volume
consolation in times of woe and tribulation.

The Israelites iu the folly of their hearts
demanded a king, in opposition to the
wishes of the Almighty. They got one
in Saul who wa9 commanded "to go and
?mite the Amorites, and utterly destroy
all they have, and spare them not; but
slay both manand woman, infant and suck
ling, ox and sheep, camel and ass" If the
story has any moral to it as Dr. Vinton
tells it, it is that a similar duty devolved
upon our departed Chief Magistrate, and
that he, like Saul, did not execute it, and,
like Saul, lost his position and his life.

If Dr. Vinton believes that Mr. Lincoln
was "unfitted" for "the second phase of
reconstruction," and that God has raised
up a more fitting instrument in his
successor, it would be at least seemly to
wait until Mr. Lincoln is in his grave
before finding fault with the dead for
the quality of mercy which comes like
the gentle dew from heaven, and through
which we all hope to be forgiven. It is
no part of our purpose to explain the
sanguinary passages of the Old
Testament, so frequently repeated by those
who iu the uame of religion commit
crimes from which the savage shrinks,
but surely it would tiot be difficult
for a clergymau to find in the sacred
writings a lesson more fittiug for these
gloomy days than that which Pr Vinton
took the labor of expounding for his

hearers last evening. The Reverend
doctor failed in his purpose if he did not
t?eud his hearers away with more
bitterness and hatred in their hearts for their
fellows tliau was there when they left
their homes to hear him. The men who
under cover of mourning for Mr. Lin
COLN find fault with him, and go so far
as to see in his assassination a clearer
way out of the dangers that surrounds
us, do not do justice te this people. If
texts of Scripture were in order, it
would bo easy to show that Mr. Lincoln,
in his tenderness of heart and in his
charity towards his erring fellow-count
rvjuen. resembled One greater than
Samuel? One who in tho agony of
assassination begged of the Father "to forgive
them (or they know not what they do.''
It is the example of tho Saviour, and

not the man who bowed A?;.vo to pieces,
that the Christian world ought to be
recommended to imitate, at all events by
Christiau ministers. In view of the
feeling which Dr. Vinton's spee.c!i at the
Academy was so well calculated to
excite, it will surprise nobody to hear that
an erratic layman, who followed, was
summarily silenced by quoting from a
certain sermon, which preachers iu these
days seldom reproduce, and which
declares that "Blessed are the merciful,
lbr they shall obtain mercy."

Louisville, Ky., April 15, 1865. J

S2JFZEIF OF THE WEEK.
President Lincoln Assassinated.
ATTEMPT TO MURDER SECRETARY SEWARD.
The shocking intelligence that President Lincoln
had been assassinated and an attempt made to
murder Secretary Seward was flashed over the
country, Saturday morning, and at once plunged
the nation, rejoicing over victory and anticipated
peace, into the deepest mourning. The
assassination of President Lincoln was committed at
ford's theater, in Washington, between nine and
am o'clock Friday evening. It had been
announced in the papers of that day that the
president and Gen Grant would be at the theater in the
evening, but Gen Grant left the city, and the
president went purely out of kindness, that the
people might not be disappointed, although
personally feeling a great disinclination to go. The
assassin committed the foul deed in the
president's private box, in presence of his wife and the

friends who were with him, shooting the
president in the back of the head, and, with a knife
in the other hand, severely wounding Major
Rathbone, who was with the presidential party,
and who attempted to seize and detain the
murdeier. But as soon as the assassin bad
completed his bloody work, he jumned upon the stage,
exclaiming sic semper tyraunO, and made his
escape through the stage door of the theater before
the paralyzed audience could do anything to
detain him, and, mounting a horse that was in
readiness, disappeared. The president was taken
to a private house opposite the theater, and the
best medical aid in the city summand to his
assistance. But nothing could be done for him;
the wound was mortal. He remained in a state
of insensibility during the night, surrounded by
surgeons, his cabinet, bis family and a few
personal Irieuds, and at twenty-two minutes past

seven o'clock Saturday mornrag lie died,
apparently without pain or struggle The attack on
Secretary Saward was made at his residence, and,
as near as can ba ascertained, at about the same
time as the assassination in the theater. The
would-be murderer in this case attempted to
obtain admission to the house on the pica that be
was the bearer of an important prescription from
Mr Seward's physician. The servant refused to
admit him, but he rushed by, and war
proceeding up stairs, wheu he met Frederick W. Seward,
assistant secretaiy of state, a younger son of Mr
Seward, and Mr Hansell, a messenger of the state
department, all of whom were attacked by th;
ruffian and disabled. Opening the door of Mr
Seward's chamber, he was met by George F
Robinson, Mr Seward's nurse, whom he stabbed aud
severely wounded, and then rushed to the bed

where the secretary was lying and inflicted
numerous stubs on his face and throat. The effort'
of Mr Robinson to detain the villain, and the fact
that, owing to his previous injuries, Mr Seward
had a wire net work support under his fractured
jaw, probably saved bis life. During the melee
tie rolled out upon the floor, drawing the bed
clothes after him, and the assassin, evidently
thinking his work completed, rushed from the
house, also mounted a horse that was in waiting,
and escaped before the alarm could be raised.

The wounds of the secretary, together with his
previous injuries, were at first thought to be
mortal; and it was not supposed that Frederick W.
Seward could survive the dangerous injuries
inflicted upon him. Both remained unconscious
and barely alive for hours; but both finally
revived, and the probabilities now are, wb are
happy to say, that they will live, though it may
well be doubtful if they will ever entirely recover
from their injuries. AU the others injured at
Secretary Seward's house are doing well and will
recover.

THE ASSASSINS.
The murderer of the president was J. Wilkes
Booth, the actor, son of the senior Junius Brutus
Booth, the great tragedian, and younger brother
of Elwin Booth, almost equally distinguished.
Them can be no doubt that Booth was the man.
He was well known to the actors in the theater,
aosne of whom saw and recognized -him as he
rushed ont after shooting the president; nid the
fact- that have come out about bis previous
actions and movements show conclusively that he
has for some time premeditated the deed. It was
at first thought that the same person might have
been the assailant of Secretary Seward; but the
united testimony of all who saw him at Mr
Seward's house points to quite a different man,
showing that two at least were engaged in the nefarious
plct, aud there are indications that there were

still more, aud that it was intended to make a
clean sweep of the president, vice president, Gen
Grant, and perhaps all the members of the
cabinet. But on this point the evidence is not clear,
and whatever is known to the authorities is, for
Obvious reasons, kept from the public. Another
question not vet clearly answered, and which
perhaps never will be, is the connection the rebel
leaders had with this plot. Did it originate in
Richmond, or was it got up by northern copperheads,
and was it for personal revenge aud spite, more
than in the interest of the rebellion? These
questions naturally arise in the mind of every one as
soon as the news is received. But now is not the
time to answer them. It is the time for action.

Efforts were at once set on foot by the
Washington authorities te arrest the assassins, and it was
hoped they might bo captured the same night.
Bur having so much the start, they succeeded in
escaping, though it is believed that the assassin
of .Secretary Seward was captured at his house in
Maiyland, near Washington, Tuesday morning.
His name is Surratt, and he has been fully
identified by the sou and daughter of Secretary Seward,
as well as the negro doorkeeper at Mr Seward's
house. The man called himself Paine when
arrested, and told several confused stories about
himself; and beyond the identification by Mr
Seward's household, the circumstantial evidence
against him is very strong. The whole Sarratt
family has been arrested, and Surratt himself has
been placed on board a monitor in the Potomac
for safe keeping. Numerous other arrests, of
peraons suspected of having some knowledge of or

participancyin the plot, have been made at
Washington and other places, but Booth, the principal
villain, is still at large. But the officers of the
law are not idle, and stimulated by the large
rewards, amounting tn cho aggregate to $190,000,
the capture of this ruffian, sooner or later, may
also be considered as sure. The authorities wisely
keep to themselves the intelligence they have and
the progress they make. A telegram from
Reading, Pa., Wednesday night, says that a man
recognized Booth on the cars passing ihrough
there that evening, hut, like a fool or a knave,
said nothing about it till the train was gone, and
when the train could be overt-ikon oy a special
train, Booth had got off at a way station and
disttppeared. The whole story is an improbable one,
and seems intended to throw the chase on a wrong

scent more than .inyihiug else. But though the
aasassiu of our beloved president is yet at large,
we are firm in the faith that he will he taken, and
strict justice yeTmeted out to t im. In this faith
we are content to wait.
A NATION IN MOURNING.
Tbj news of President Lincoln's death threw
the whole country into mourning; brought the
whole people from their bight of joy, to the very
depth of sorrow. Never has the death of any
one man, whatever his virtues or his station
created so profound a sensation of grief among
the whole people. There were few loyal households
in the country, North or South, where the news
was not received with tears; and whore it was
otherwise it was because the sorrow was too deep
seated and stunning to find utterance in weeping.

The sensation to every one wns of the loss of a
near and dear perso ial friend. In every city aud
town, appropriate means were taken to exhibit
a sense of the natl'n'a bereavement and to show
respect for the dead president. 1) Ils were tolled,
bnil rings public end private were draped with
the insignia of mourning, and in many places
busiueN was entirely suspended through
Saturday, and stores and shops shut up. People
wandered listlessly about tho streets, or gatherc I In
little groups to sp-Hk in subluol tones and with
aorrowftil faces of the virtues of the loved and
lost, and to utter < xecrations, not loud, but deep,
ku the murderer of the president Sunday
morning all the c.ergyuien oi the laud made the na-

tions bereavement the burden of their pravers
aud tbeir discourses, and there were few churches
notwithstanding it wu< Easter, the most
joyful festival of the church, that were not
decorated with the signs of grief and mourning.
Legislative and municipal bodies took the earliest
opportunity to pay their tribute of respect to Mr
Lincoln's memory, and to adjourn. The
Massachusetts legislature did not meet till Monday,
from the over Fast day adjournment, and after
hearing an eloquent message from Governor
Andrew, and passing resolutions suitable to the
occasion, adjourned again, without transacting other
business, till after the president's funeral. The
New York assembly, almost ths only other state
legislature in session, also took appropriate
notice of the event, and the city government of
Springfield and other cities took advantage of their
first meeting after the sad event, to pay every mark

of respect and affection in there power to Mr
Lincoln's memory. In the midst of the national
sorrow, a few w'ere found base and traitorous enough
to openly rejoice and exult in the president's
murder. Such were hardly dealt with. A. man in
Washington was shot for saying he was glad Mr
Lincoln was dead, and in other places men were,
severely beaten, or were imprisoned by the police
to save their lives; and wo are sotry to say that
some women were found toexult instead of weep.

At San Francisco democratic newspapers were
mobbed, and in other places committees of
citizens took upon themselves the unwarrantable
liberty of arresting persons on mere suspicion and
making them declare themselves on the national
and popular side. But to the credit of the people
be it said that these acts of violence were few,
and but a handful was discovered in the whole
North to rejoice over a deed so dastardly. And
at Richmond, Petersburg aud other places lately
captured from the rebels, the sensation was uo
less profound, and the grief little less apparent
than at the North The ronel genera! Lee was
deeply affected. "It has put the war back to tbo
fail of Sumter;" "the Ssutb|iias lost her best
friend," were the expressions with which hitherto
prominent rebels received the news, while the
poorer classes, and especially the freedmen, hid

no words to express their horror and woe. But,
and what is remarkable,! while everybody
mourned none were terrified or despondent. The
universal sentiment was that whoever might die,
the republic still lived, and would live. Our
safety or prosperity is not dependent on the life of
one man, be he ever so great or good. There was
no panic in gold or stocks. After the first burst
of grief business went on in the usual channels;
and now, save that dull, throbbing heart- ache,,
everythingmoves on as before. The people mourn
for their lost ruler, bat they give their confidence
to tho new one, and trust in God io bring us safely
through the dangers that surround us. The
feeling in Canada aud the provinces produced by the
sad event, is also worchv of note. Iu Montreal,
Toronto, Halifax and otherplac.es, the horror and

grief at the assassination were only less than in
the United States, aud everything possible was
done, privately and officially to assure us of the
sympathy of our northern neighbors. We rejoice
in this, aind trust it is the dawn of a better feeling
than has before existed since the war commenced
between the two countries.

THE FUNERAL SERVICES.
The president's funeral was observed at
Washington on Wednesday. The principal religions
services were held at the White House, Dr
Hall reading the Scriptures, Bishop Simpson
making the opening prayer, Rev Dr Gurley, the
late president's pastor, delivering the funeral
discourse, and R;v Dr Gray, formerly of Shelburne
Falls, now of Washington, making the conclud- .
ing prayer. Accommodations were furnished for
690 at the White House, and those in attendance
comprised the principal officers of the
government, the foreign mnisters, members of
Cangre s and representatives of the different state
governments. At the close of the religious
services at the White House, the remains were taken
to the Rotunda of the Capitol, where further
brief services were performed. The funeral
procession consisted of an imposing military escort,
including a detachment of colored troops, and
then followed in the mourning train, besides
personal friends, the diplomatic\corps, the officers of

the departments, Congress, governors and
prominent men from every state, borides avast crowd of
untitled and undistinguished but sincerely
mourning citizens. The procession was by far fie
largest and mo-t imposing ever seen in Washington,
and occupied an hour and a half in passing any
given point. Among the pall-bearcrs was Hon
George Ashmun of this city and Hon Henry L.
Dawes of I'ittsfieltL member of Congress from
this district, and aiming the mourners were Gov
Andrew of Massachusetts and Gov Buckingham
of Connecticut. The president's remains were to
start Friday for Spn me field, 111., where they are
to repose near his old home. They wll travel
slowly, taking Baltimore, Philadelphia, New
YorkJ Albany, Buffalo and other places in the
route, and at these and other principal places
opportunity will be given the public to view the
face of their beloved president. An attempt his

been made to have the funeral route embrace this
city, but it seems doubtful if that plan can be
adopted. The day of the president's funeral was
observed all over the country as a day of
mourning. All business was suspended in accordance
with the general wish of the people, no less than
tire terms of an official request to thateffect.
Almost every building, public or private, had some
signs or tokens of mourning upon it, and there
would much more have been done in the way of
decorations had not the supply of black material
in the country of all kinds been exhausted before
the demand'was half supplied. In Springfield
the citizens met in their respective places of
worship at noon, and every one was filled. In the
afternoon there was a mass meeting at the City
Hall, where were appropriate services, including

a speech by Mayor Briggs and an eloquent and
touching eulogy by Dr J. G. Holland. I lie crowd
in attendance could not halt get into the hull,
and an open air meeting was organized, with
ex-Mayor Bemis td preside, and addresses by Rev
Messrs Seely e and Potter. A salute of 18 guns
was fired at the armory in the morning, w th a
national salute of 86 eunsat evening, and half
hour gnns during the day; -and the
number of people abroad, and the sober and
decorous appearance of all, showed that the day
was one of mourning in reality as well as in name.

The record of the transactions in one place on
that eventful day is the history of ail. It was
the same all over the country. The busy country
stood still, and everyone was glad to give up one
day, and to show every mark of love aud respect
to'our dead president's mimory. No one uow
living is likely to see such a day again, and ail
will sincerely hope that there may never lie
occasion for its like.
THE NEW ADMINISTRATION.
According to the provisions of the constitution

main* iu Philadelphia. j
Sunday and the day previous afforded the |
publie an opportunity of testing the affection ;
in which President Lincoln was held by the j
people while living, and the effect that his
assassipation has produced on the public mind. !
Saturday the population turned ont to do
honor to his remains, and on Sunday there was a
living line of people, from early in the
morning, extending from the Delaware to the
Schuylkill, a distance of two miles, marching
c«)iitiuu»lly in procession to the place where
his honored remains were deposited, desirous
of taking their last look of one who basso
largely filled the measure of their and their
country's approbation. It was a novel
spectacle to see all grades and conditions of society,
all sexes and ages, moving decorously along iti

that living human stream, animated by the one
impulse, reverence for the memory of the chief
whom they hud entrusted with power for four
years, and whose title to it they had renewed
for another term, so satisfied had they been
with the patriotism, the wisdom and the be*
nevolence with which he hud exercised it.
The procession, as it passed through the streets,
was the most solemn and impressive spectacle
ever witnessed in this country. The mournful
music, the draped flags,
the soldiers, the muffled
knells from the church towers, the melancholy
booming of the minute-guns, the silent march,
and all the accessories spoke in sad tones of the
sincerity and universality of the public grief.

No one who saw that mournful pro«
ever have it obliterated from his memory.
President Lincoln's remains left
Philadelphia at a quarter past three Monday morning.

and Jersey City. Governor Parker received
them at Trenton. They were lying in state
during Monday afternoon and night at the
New York City Hall, and were visited by great
crowds. Tuesday a vast funeral procession
conducted them to the Albany cars, and at
Union .Square George Bancroft pronounced a
funeral oration. The interment ot the remains
at Springfield will he upon May Gth.
Thursday, May 26th, is appointed by President
Johnson a day of mourning for President Lincoln.

BKBrOBD PA" FRIDAY, APRILS, 1865.
THIS LESSON AND THE DUTY OF
THE DAY.
The President of the United States has
perished by the hand of an assassin. It
was not personal motive, it was not private
revenge, which prompted this deed.of blood
It was partisan hate, it was political
ferocity, which stirred the assassin's heart, and
raised his parricidal hand. It was the same
diabolical spirit which beat down Sumuer in
the Senate chamber, which murdered and
pillaged in Kansas, which conspired for the
assassination of Mr. Lincoln on his way to
the capital, which poured shot and shell
in* Fort Sumter, which fought with our
troops in the streets of Baltimore, which
butchered the garrison of Fort Pillow,
which wrought the atrocities of Quantrell
in the streets of Lawrence, and which
starved eur soldiers in southern prisons.
Nothing but the fiendish malignity which slavery

begets could contrive and effect the murder
ofthe Chief Magistrate in the presence of his
wife, and aim a bowie-knife at the throat of
an old man stretched on a sick bed and
enfeebled by wounds. Slavery, after having
filled the land with war, and mourning, and
lamentation, now in its death agony
completes the record of its infamy by the most
brutal assassination. This is the lesson of
the day.

What are its duties? They are first to
take care of the republic. The succession
of the Presidential office is amply provided
for by the constitution And the laws. There
can be no interregnum. The functions of
the magistracy are silently transmitted from
one person to another. The office never
dies; there is a living hand always to bear
it. It is one of the felicities of our
political system, that office can never fell into the
hands of a child. There is always a man
for it, chosen beforehand of the people.

And while it is a mistake to suppose that
the personal character of the officer has not
much to do with the administration of the
office, it is nevertheless true that the
President is so hedged about with other
independent authorities, and these are all so
responsible to the people, that the real safety
of the people is after all in their own
hands.

There is, moreover, an influence of public
opinion, all-pervading and all-powerful, by
which our Government, more than any
other, is swayed, .and which proportionately
lessens the importance of any individual
man, however pure and wise. Mr. Lincoln
had the wisdom to study and the sagacity
to follow public opinion, which was, in fact,
the great secret of his marvellous succete.
His successor must follow his example, and
the pohey which he pursues must be the
policy indicated by the nation's matured
thought and will.

Besides all these, we have an element of
vitality which no other Government enjoys.
This lies in the state sovereignties, for
sovereignties we prefer to call them, qualified
though they be. With them rests
especially the conservation of order and the protec- j
tion of private rights. It is owing to them
and to the vast power which they have
exited for the equipoise of the political iorces
the dreadful strain of this civil war. To

these great powers we may confidently look
hereafter for the balance of our system, and
that the heresy of secession and the
extravagance of paramount state rights are
generally condemned and laid aside.
Taking courage from these reflections, let
us give a generous confidence to the new
President, upon whom is devolved, in this
hour of our bereavement, the great trust of
his honored and lamented predecessor. -
Graver responsibilities have rarely fallen
upon man. In an instant the task is put
upon him of composing the greatest civil
war in history, after the principal battles
have been fought, but while the elements
are yet in disorder. Let us give him our
confidence and our counsel. He is at once
our Chief Magistrate and our servant. The
responsibility is more with us than with
him. Let us confide in him and act with

Another of the duties of the day is to
search out and punish the assassins and all
their aiders and abettors, whoever and
wherever they may be. A crime like this
must not go unpunished; but let everything
be done according to law. All irregular
violence is itself a crime, whether animated by
one man or by a conclave of conspirators, or
by a mob. The country has its laws for the
Government of all its people, and he or they
who infringe them by tumult or a breach of
the peace, rebel against the nation. Let us
be resolute and inflexible, but let us be
orderly and oalni.

TREATMENT OF THE REBEL
LEADERS.
Those persons who are simple enough to
believe that Gen. Lee and the other rebel
leaders, military or civil, will be converted
into good Union citizens, by any conciliatory
measures, do not understand the character
nor the feelings of such arch traitors. The
, favorable terms granted to them by General
Grant have already been broken by them in
the spirit, if not In the letter of the terms of
capitulation. The letter writers from
Richmond and Baltimore, speak of the
unqualified impudence of some of the rebel officers
wearing their swords and some of them
loaded pistols, and all their uniforms, with
a strut and bluster as if they still had the
power to make their own will the law of the
land. Kindness is thrown away upon such
men. They have such an overweening idea

of their own importance, that they act as if
they believed that it was to their own merit
tliat a concession was made when they were
allowed to surrender, and not out of
compassion to their weakness.
When they are treated as a conquered
people, and are made to feel that they are
rebels, and their lives depend upon the
mercy of the Government , and that those who
show by their actions that they have aot
repented of their treason will suffer the
penalty of the law as traitors, then, and not
before, will their impudence be restrained, and
they either be content to remain in
obscurity pursuing some honest employment,
or leave a.country to which they have been
a disgrace & ed a curse.

Point, and his association with Northern
men, has given him tire manners of a
gentleman, and prevents him from showing the
bravado and vulgar insolence so prevalent
aiaoßg his officers. In principle 'he is no
better than the worst of the rebels in the

Gen. Lee is equally responsible with Jeff
Davis for the treatment our soldiers received
when captured as prisoners of war *by the
army under his command. He knew the
treatment to which they were subjected in
Libby Prison, Castle Thunder and Belle
Island. We have no evidence that he ever
objected to it, and year after year, as his
army was successful in taking prisoners,
ivhich by the laws of war he was bound and
g-overened as every other civilized man, to

treat with all the kindness consistent with
security from escape, he delivered over to be
treated with an inhumanity which has no
parallel in the annals of civilized
No one can believe that if Gen. Lee desired
t hat our prisoners should have been treated
ovlherwis j, it would not have been done.
Will any of his admirers deny he could not
ha tie prevented the colored soldiers taken in
bat* "le from being sent to work upon the
fortifications near Richmond, and yet that was
done and persisted in until some of the F.

F. V's. in our hands as prisoners, were
subject in retalliation to like treatment by Gen.
Butler. When two of our officers had been
piaced r.n dungeons in Richmond and
ordered that the son of Gen. Lee and another
F. F. V., then our prisoners of war, be held
as hostages, and notified Jeff Davis that
they would be treated in the same manner
as he should treat the Union officers, Gen.
Lee had the Union officers released. What
his affection 'as a father could induce him to
do to save hit own son, his duty as a soldier
a General and a man, should have induced
him to do for the prisoners-of-war taken in
battle by men under hiscommand, and whom'
he knew were subjected to the torture of
slow starvation, and the most inhuman
treatment, and even butchered in cold blood.

He has never shown by his conduct or his
orders that what was done to our prisoners
has ever been disapproved of by him, and it
is too late now, when his power to do evil
has been broken, to deny his participation
in the guilt, nor avoid the infamy which
must forever cling to him as one who
deliberately allowed his prisoners-of-war to be
subjected to a treatment that would surely
and certainly lead to imbecility, disease and
death.

The rebels in the South and the
Copperheads in the North, may extol Gen. Lee a3
the finest soldier of their so called
Confederacy, and a most gallant gentleman, but
every right thinking man and the civilized
world, will consider such terms when
applied to him, in the same light as the term
"first gentleman in Europe" that the
admirers of George IV, applied to him in his
life time, but who is now condemed as one
of the greatest brutes and most heartless
scoundrels that ever disgraced a throne. -
Miner's Journal.

A UNITED PEOPLE. - It really seems as if
the sacrifice of Abraham Lincoln's life was
providentially ordered, to bring about
perfect unanimity among the people of this
country. All partisan feeling has ceaeed
among us. Evei 7 house in the land is a
house of mourning". The and
universal grief has ma de us all brothers,
sorrowing as for the lot is of a beloved father.
The consciences of tnose who once derided
and .abused Abraham' Lincoln have been
sorely smitten, and we believe there is a
sincere determination that the head of the
government, in a time of civil war, shall no
longer be the object of partisan opposition.

President Johnson, judging by present
appearances, will be supported by the people
with a degree nf unanimity unknown since
the time of Washington. The plotters of
the late infamous crime have brought about
a result they could never have dreamed of.
They have united the loyal people as they
have never been united before. In all
measures necessary to finish the work of
President Lincoln, President Johnson will have
the support of all parties. - Phila. Bulletin.

PRESIDENT JOHNSO.N'S ADDRESSES. -
Nothing could be more appropriate and
becoming, in tone and sentin'ent, than the
addresses which Mr. Johnson has been called
on to make since the duties t'f the
Presidency devolved upon him. Thep are weighty
in manner and in matter. 1 hey indicate
unmistakably that solemn sense of
responsibility which is the best guarantee for the
faithful discharge of his high trust. His
reserve in speaking of specific acts of
administration is especially considerate and wise.
In declaring that he shall act upon each
question as it may arise, and as it may at the
time seem best, he lays down the golden
rule of all wise statesmanship and givea
strong assurance that the government will
be administered with strict regard to the
practical necessities and emergencies of the
hour.

W i find this remarkable paragraph in a
Western paper: "About eight miles from
Shelbyville, Indiana, is the little town of
Marietta, a place noted for nothing in particular,
save the virulent type of copperheadism
prevailing there. The reception of the dreadful
news from Washington set the honest
Democrats thereabouts crazy with joy. In the
absence of a cannon they loaded and fired an

comrades swung him up by the neck, so that his

eternity. Others who expressed their
gratification at the news were served likewise.
